prompt: What does the principle of least privilege say?

choices.text: Give administrators every permission so they are never blocked
choices.why: That is the opposite of the principle.

choices.text: Only the access the task needs, for as long as it needs it
choices.why: Right. Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975.

choices.text: Trust nobody on the staff with any access at all
choices.why: People still get what their work needs.

choices.text: Grant access first and remove it if something goes wrong
choices.why: That is how privilege creep starts.

prompt: "I trust my staff, so why limit them?" What does the lesson answer?
hint: Most of what goes wrong is not the person.

choices.text: Staff should not be trusted, since insiders cause every incident
choices.why: The lesson says the principle is not about honesty.

choices.text: Trust is fine, and limits slow people down for nothing
choices.why: The limits shrink the damage of a leak, a bug or a mistake.

choices.text: It limits the damage of a leak, a bug or a mistake
choices.why: Right. A smaller blast radius.

choices.text: Auditors demand it whatever the staff are like
choices.why: The lesson's reason is the damage, not the audit.

prompt: How far the damage from one failure spreads is called its blast ___.
The person packing orders is given customers' delivery addresses but not their purchase history. Which idea is that?

choices.text: Need to know
choices.why: Right. Only the part the current task requires.

choices.text: Separation of duties between packing and sales
choices.why: That splits a task between two people; here one person gets less data.

choices.text: Default deny on the shop's network firewall
choices.why: The network is not involved.

choices.text: Isolation of the packing station in a container
choices.why: No program is being isolated.

prompt: ps showed the portal running as shop rather than root. Why does that matter?
hint: What could a bug do as root?

choices.text: Programs run faster under ordinary accounts than as root
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: A bug in the portal is confined to shop's permissions
choices.why: Right. As root, it would control the server.

choices.text: root cannot listen on port 80
choices.why: root can; the point is not needing root.

choices.text: Customers see the account name in the page
choices.why: Nothing on the page shows it.

prompt: getpcaps printed cap_net_bind_service for the portal. What problem does that one capability solve?

choices.text: It lets the portal read the salaries file when finance asks
choices.why: The portal still cannot read it.

choices.text: It encrypts the portal's traffic on the network
choices.why: Capabilities are not encryption.

choices.text: Listening on a low port without being root
choices.why: Right. One piece of root's power, and nothing else.

choices.text: It lets ana restart the portal through sudo
choices.why: That is ana's sudo rule, not the portal's capability.

prompt: ana runs IT and has an account on www. Why was she refused the salaries file?
hint: Running IT is not a reason.

choices.text: Her account was disabled
choices.why: She ran commands with it.

choices.text: She is neither its owner nor in hr
choices.why: Right. Read access is for bruno and the hr group.

choices.text: IT staff are always refused everything on servers
choices.why: She is allowed two commands as root.

choices.text: The file was locked because bruno had it open
choices.why: Linux permissions, not a lock, refused her.

prompt: Why would a sudo rule allowing ana to run vim as root defeat the purpose of her narrow rule?
hint: What can an editor do from inside?

choices.text: vim is slower when it runs as root
choices.why: Speed is irrelevant.

choices.text: vim refuses to run under sudo
choices.why: It runs; that is the problem.

choices.text: Editors cannot open log files
choices.why: They open any file root can.

choices.text: vim runs other commands, so it is root in full
choices.why: Right. A shell or an editor hands over everything.

prompt: sudo -l cat /srv/hr/salaries.csv printed nothing and exit 1. What did that tell ana?
hint: -l followed by a command asks a question.

choices.text: That command is not allowed for her
choices.why: Right. Asked without running it.

choices.text: The salaries file is empty
choices.why: Nothing was read; the question was about permission.

choices.text: cat is not installed on www
choices.why: bruno ran cat on the same machine.

choices.text: sudo needs her password before answering any question
choices.why: It answered without one.

prompt: What does separation of duties limit?

choices.text: What one account may touch on one server
choices.why: That is least privilege.

choices.text: How much data a backup holds
choices.why: Unrelated.

choices.text: What one person can do alone
choices.why: Right. A sensitive task needs two people.

choices.text: How many programs may run as root on one machine
choices.why: That is not the idea.

prompt: An email that looks like a supplier's asks the shop to update its bank account. What defence does the lesson give?

choices.text: A stronger spam filter on the shop's email
choices.why: It helps, and the lesson's defence is a second person.

choices.text: A second person calls the supplier on a known number first
choices.why: Right. A call before the money moves.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking whether it is genuine
choices.why: The reply goes to whoever sent it.

choices.text: Encrypt the payment file before sending it
choices.why: The payment would still go to the wrong account.

prompt: Match each arrangement to its name.

pairs.left: two people must act together, like two keys turned at once
somebody else does the job for a while

prompt: With nine people, only ana can load firewall changes. What does the lesson say the shop does instead of strict separation?
hint: The second person arrives after the fact.

choices.text: Nothing, since a small shop is exempt
choices.why: No exemption; the control changes form.

choices.text: It hires a second network administrator
choices.why: That is one option, not what the lesson describes.

choices.text: Every change goes into a log the owners read weekly
choices.why: Right. Detective rather than preventive.

choices.text: ana stops changing the firewall
choices.why: The firewall still needs changing.

prompt: Order these from the weakest isolation to the strongest.
trap: A container shares the host's kernel; a virtual machine has its own; an air gap has no connection at all.

prompt: A flaw in the host's kernel lets a program escape. Where does the lesson say it stays inside instead?
hint: Which level has its own kernel?

choices.text: In a container
choices.why: A container shares the host's kernel, so the flaw is shared too.

choices.text: In a virtual machine
choices.why: Right. Its own kernel keeps the flaw inside.

choices.text: In a separate user account
choices.why: Accounts rely on that same kernel.

choices.text: In a sandboxed browser tab
choices.why: A sandbox also runs on the host's kernel.

prompt: Which program at the shop deserves the most isolation, by the lesson's rule?

choices.text: The spreadsheet bruno uses for salaries
choices.why: Valuable, and it reads no input from strangers.

choices.text: The script that restarts the portal
choices.why: Only ana runs it.

choices.text: The firewall's rule file
choices.why: It is a file, read by fw, written by ana.

choices.text: The code that processes files customers upload
choices.why: Right. It reads input from strangers.

prompt: Match each event to what should happen to access.

pairs.right: the role's standard access, nothing more
the new role's access granted and the old one's removed
every account disabled on the last day

right_distractors: the same access as a colleague, to be safe

prompt: Who should confirm or remove the entries in an access review of the finance folder?

choices.text: bruno, the folder's owner
choices.why: Right. The owner knows who needs it.

choices.text: ana, since IT manages the server
choices.why: IT knows the server, not who in packing needs finance's folder.

choices.text: Each user, for their own access
choices.why: People rarely give access back on their own.

choices.text: An auditor, once a year, for every folder
choices.why: An auditor checks the review was done.

prompt: ana needs root on www twice a month. What does just-in-time access change?
hint: A stolen password works on how many days?

choices.text: She gets root permanently, but with a longer password
choices.why: That is still standing privilege.

choices.text: She loses root and asks bruno to do the work
choices.why: bruno runs finance, not servers.

choices.text: Root is granted for hours when needed, then removed
choices.why: Right. A stolen password is useless the other days.

choices.text: Root is shared with the other staff so somebody always has it
choices.why: That multiplies standing privilege.

prompt: Which of these reduce standing privilege or creep? Choose all that apply.
hint: Taking access away is the hard half.

choices.text: Removing the old role's access when somebody moves
choices.why: The mover's second half.

choices.text: Periodic access reviews by the data's owner
choices.why: Catches what nobody removed.

choices.text: Copying a colleague's access for a new joiner
choices.why: That imports the colleague's creep.

choices.text: Giving every administrator permanent root
choices.why: That is standing privilege.

prompt: Malware arrives in an email ana opens. Why does the lesson want her reading email from an ordinary account?
hint: It runs as whoever opened it.

choices.text: Ordinary accounts receive less spam than administrator accounts
choices.why: Spam volume is not the point.

choices.text: It inherits only an everyday user's rights
choices.why: Right. Not the keys to the shop.

choices.text: Administrators are not allowed to have email at all
choices.why: They can; they use an ordinary account for it.

choices.text: It makes ana's password longer
choices.why: Account type does not change password length.
